Use a one-pass map from values to earlier indices. For each index i, first look up target − nums[i]; if present, return that earlier index and i. Otherwise, store nums[i] and continue. This takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

The invariant is that before processing i, the map contains only values from indices less than i. That guarantees distinct indices, and when the later member of the valid pair is reached, its partner is already in the map.

Duplicates work, including [3,3] with target 6, because lookup happens before insertion. Zero, negative values, and a two-element array work the same way. Empty arrays, single-element arrays, and inputs without a valid pair violate the stated guarantee; no fallback behavior is specified. For solve(prices), scan left to right, tracking the lowest earlier price and the best profit. At each price, first evaluate selling against the lowest earlier price, then update that minimum—this ensures the buy precedes the sell.

Invariant: after each processed price, the minimum is the lowest price seen, and the best profit is the maximum valid profit within the processed prefix, never below zero. Every possible selling day is checked against its cheapest earlier buying day.

Boundary cases: empty or single-price input returns zero because no transaction is possible; decreasing or equal prices also return zero. Repeated minimum prices work normally. For [7,1,5,3,6,4], buying at 1 and later selling at 6 gives 5.

Time: O(n). Extra space: O(1).
